Situated on rock outcrop at the W edge of a N-S ravine (Wth of top c. 100m). A low grass-covered cairn (dims 31.5m N-S; c. 9.5m E-W; max. H 1m) contains a chamber (L 2.4m; Wth 2.2m; H 0.85m) at the S end composed of two portal-stones, two sidestones, a backstone and roofstone. The passage tombs (LE025-093001-; LE025-093002-) and a cairn (LE025-093003-) lie c. 120m to the S. Two globular glacial erratics (dims c. 1.2m x 0.9m; H 1m), 2m apart, form a rough N-S alignment. The S stone has a natural vertical channel (Wth 0.1m; D 0.2m) extending the length of its N face. In local folklore as recorded in the Schools’ Manuscripts feuding giants on Sheebeg and Sheemore threw stones at each other but both missiles fell short and landed here. Situated on the highest point at the S end of the N-S ridge of Sheebeg Hill. It is depicted on the 1835 and 1907 editions of the OS 6-inch map where it is described as ‘Fin Mc Cool’s Monument’. This is a grass- and scrub-covered flat-topped cairn of limestone boulders (diam. of base 38m; diam. of top 12.9m; H 5m). It has an oblong depression on the summit (L 12m; D 1m), the result of investigations in 1931 when a closed chamber of megalithic orthostats, containing two skeletons, was briefly opened (Irish Times, 7 January 1931; Gilligan 2015). It was reputed in the local folklore to be the burial place of Fionn Mac Cumhaill, which also records the 1931 investigation, for which see this web-page accessed on 06/04/2017: http://www.duchas.ie/en/cbes/4649689/4647538 It is listed as a passage tomb (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 143; Herity 1974, 279, Le 8).

LE033-027----:
Situated in a low-lying position in a N-S valley between drumlins. This is a well-preserved but overgrown two-chambered portal tomb (dims 3.7m E-W; 1.85m N-S) with the portals (max. H 1.4m) and sillstone at W. The front chamber (dims 2.3m E-W; 1.85-2.1m N-S) has single sidestones, but a low septal-stone separates it from the inner chamber (dims 1.4m E-W; 2.85m N-S) which has single sidestones and two backstones. There is no visible cairn or roofstone. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 79)

Situated on a gentle S-facing spine overlooking a low-lying basin to the S. An overgrown area with several upright stones suggests the remains of a two-chambered gallery (dims 7m NE-SW; 1.5m NW-SE) which probably formed a court tomb. Seven contiguous stones, including one jamb-stone at E, on the SE side of the gallery survive with two jamb-stones from the NW side. There are some traces of a cairn but field stones have been added to it. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 80-81)

Located in pasture on the S extremity of a low and narrow N-S ridge overlooking a low-lying basin. A tapered gallery, probably of two chambers originally, is aligned N-S (L 4.5m; Wth 1.65 at N; 1.3m at S). Located towards the bottom of the W-facing slope of a N-S drumlin ridge. A small feature is depicted on the S side of an E-W drain only on the 1907 edition of the OS 6-inch map where it is described as a ‘Giant’s Grave’ and on the 1945 revision where it is described as a ‘Megalith’.  Three slabs form a triangle (dims c. 3.4m N-S; c. 6m E-W) and may be the remains of a megalithic tomb. The N stone (dims 1.1m x 0.4m) is 3.7m from the S stone (dims 1.6m x 0.5m; H 0.45m), and a third prone slab is c. 5.5m W of the S stone. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 86)

Situated on a gentle W-facing slope and just S of an E-W road. It is depicted only on the 1907 and 1945 editions of the OS 6-inch map where it is described as a ‘Grave Yard’. This is a scrub-covered, wedge-shaped area (dims 9m NE-SW; 4.5m NW-SE at NE to 9.5m at SW) defined by a line (L 6.7m) of nine contiguous upright slabs (H 0.3-0.8m) at the NW edge and seven on the SE side, but only four on the SE side remain standing. Some of the fallen stones are larger (L 1.3m; 2m) and might have been lintels. No internal structural stones are visible but one large kerbstone (L 2.55m x 0.35-0.5m; H 0.7m) is at the SW end. It is very likely to be a wedge tomb.

LE036-012----:
Situated at the crest of a NW-facing slope. The tomb on McKenna’s land was widely known locally and it was described in the local folklore during the 1930s (IFC: vol. 0214, 332; 0220, 23-4; 022, 588-9). A large stone (dims 3m NW-SE; 2.6m NE-SW; T 0.2-0.4m) is resting on a single orthostat (dims 0.8m x 0.2m; H 1m) with another orthostat (dims 1m x 0.2m; H 1.2m) adjacent. The back of the large stone rests on the ground on the W side of a N-S field bank. The stone is surrounded by an overgrown cairn (diam. c. 20m; H c. 1m) which survives only W of the field bank.

Located on a gentle W-facing slope in an undulating landscape. This is a rectangular chamber (dims 2.5m ENE-WSW; 1.2m NNW-SSE; H 1.55m) consisting of two portal-stones at E, two sidestones and a backstone with a single roofstone (dims 2.2m x 2.1m; T 0.5m). There may have been traces of a cairn (H 1m), which could be field clearance, surrounding it at S. It was incorporated into the junction of two field banks, but it is now accessible directly from the ENE-WSW public road at S. (de Valera and Ó Nualláin 1972, 81)
